context.situation: On 17 June 2018 a US-listed rent-to-own retailer (Company A) signed a definitive merger agreement to be acquired by an acquisition vehicle (Buyer B) formed by a private investment firm, with a financial-services firm committed as equity and debt participant. The deal was publicly announced the next day.
terms: All-cash offer for every outstanding share; total transaction value approximately US$1.4 billion including debt (approximate).
Company A's board unanimously approved the agreement and resolved to recommend stockholder approval.
Buyer B delivered equity commitment letters and a limited guarantee from its sponsors; debt commitment letters were in place. The transaction is not subject to a financing condition.

Closing conditions: Company A stockholder approval; expiry or termination of the HSR antitrust waiting period and other antitrust approvals; no law or order prohibiting the merger; accuracy of representations and warranties; performance of covenants; no material adverse effect.

Outside (End) Date: 17 December 2018. If the merger has not become effective and either the governmental-antitrust-consent condition or the no-legal-restraint condition remains unsatisfied on that date, either party may extend the End Date to 17 March 2019 by written notice delivered to the other party by 11:59 p.m. Eastern on 17 December 2018. Following that extension, either party may extend to 17 June 2019 by written notice delivered by 11:59 p.m. Eastern on 17 March 2019. A party whose breach causes failure to close by the End Date cannot terminate under the End Date clause.

A reverse termination fee in the low hundreds of millions of US dollars (roughly 9% of announced transaction value including net debt, approximate) is payable by Buyer B to Company A in specified termination circumstances, guaranteed by the sponsors.
A company termination fee is payable by Company A in specified circumstances, including a superior-proposal termination.
The parties publicly stated they expected the transaction to close by the end of 2018.
known_unknowns: Whether and when the HSR waiting period will expire or a second request will be issued.
Whether stockholders will approve the merger.
Company A's operating performance between signing and closing and its effect on either party's willingness to close.
Whether either party will exercise, or fail to exercise, the End Date extension right.

assumptions: Completion by 31 Dec 2018 requires both HSR clearance and stockholder approval within about 6.5 months of signing. That is achievable if no second request is issued, but a second request typically adds several months.

The two-step End Date extensions run to June 2019 and are tied specifically to antitrust or legal-restraint conditions. Together with an unusually large reverse termination fee (~9% of transaction value), this suggests the parties expected material antitrust or regulatory risk. That lowers the chance of a clean 2018 close below the typical base rate for sponsor take-privates.
Financing is committed and there is no financing condition, so financing failure is not the main risk to closing in 2018. Regulatory timing and buyer willingness to proceed are.

A rent-to-own retailer's operating performance could shift during the pendency period. That could affect the buyer's appetite to close, for example by letting the outside date lapse or declining to extend, given the termination mechanics.
Stockholder approval is likely given the unanimous board recommendation and an all-cash premium offer, absent a competing bid.
The parties' public expectation of closing by end-2018 is treated as moderately informative but typically optimistic.
answer.most_informative_observation: Whether the FTC issued a second request under HSR, or whether the HSR waiting period expired without one, in the months after filing.
answer.recognition_note: I believe this is Rent-A-Center's June 2018 agreement to be acquired by an affiliate of Vintage Capital, with B. Riley participating. I recall the deal did not close and the agreement was terminated around the December 2018 End Date, followed by a dispute over the reverse termination fee. That recollection could bias me, so I have tried to base the probability only on the supplied terms. A purely terms-based estimate might be modestly higher.

outcome.summary: Neither party delivered the End Date extension notice required by 11:59 p.m. Eastern on 17 December 2018. The company terminated the merger agreement on 18 December 2018 and demanded the US$126.5 million reverse termination fee. The buyer sued to enforce the agreement; on 14 March 2019 the Delaware Court of Chancery ruled the termination valid; on 22 April 2019 the parties announced a US$92.5 million settlement. The merger was never consummated.
